When dreams outgrow the individual Some of the clearest evidence that dreams are not purely personal comes from moments of collective stress. Dur- ing the early days of pandemic lock- downs in 2020, sleep researchers across several countries noted a marked spike in vivid, often bizarre dreaming, a phe- nomenon the press quickly nicknamed the pandemic dream surge. People with no connection to one another reported eerily similar imagery: empty streets, in- visible threats, separation from loved ones. The dreams were personal in de- tail but shared in structure, shaped by a fear that belonged to everyone at once. This suggests dreams may function less like private diaries and more like weather systems, forming in response to the pressure of the surrounding at- mosphere. The dreamer supplies the local detail. The conditions supply the storm. History offers similar echoes in quieter times too, soldiers on opposite sides of long wars have described strik- ingly similar dreams of home, of rivers, of mothers calling them back, as though fear and longing draw from the same well no matter which uniform a person wears.
